chapter: Howard Johnson and the loft scene
title: Howard Johnson's group Substructure and learning to improvise on tuba
summary: Joining Johnson's tuba ensemble, getting his calls, and Johnson's method of adding to written tuba parts.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: interesting things on the tuba. So he came in and he just like shattered my thoughts of what a tuba can do in a improvisational setting, or a setting where the music is not written down or structured and everything. Where I’m not playing a tuba part but I’m actually doing what the saxophones and everybody else is doing. I’m given the freedom to improvise and do all types of things. So Howard kind of reset my mind, and then I was also able to join his group at that time it was called Substructure. It was a group of six tubas and now it’s called Gravity. So I was around other great tuba players that were improvising and everything. And then Howard, he was picking up so much work that he began to like okay I can no longer do this but I have somebody, you know, and then he would throw a recommendation to me. And then I’d come into the setting and everything and then when you come into a setting like following like an innovator, they expect you to be an innovator. So you couldn’t come in following a great, great musician like that and be less than he was. Because they figure the reason you got the gig is because you can do what he did. And even though I couldn’t do a lot of what he could do, I began to work and began to improvise and everything, and developed certain types of skills and everything. So I began to get calls from everybody that was on the scene that wanted a tuba. And most of the time they just wanted you to do whole notes and everything. And I learned this from Howard you know, when guys write for the tuba they kind of say okay, I’ll give him a whole note here then give him a bunch of rests so he can get his breath then give him another whole note here. And then maybe give him — oh a half note. And maybe four quarter notes. And then I’ll give him four eighth notes but they’ll have to be scale wide [scats]. I mean very simplistic parts. But what Howard used to do, and what he taught us to do is that you know you play the guy’s music first. And then you just quietly begin to add things to it. You know you add this, add this into it, and then you just look up at the guy and if he’s looking at you and nodding then you begin to add more, add more, add more and everything. And this is what Howard did in the Gil Evans orchestra when he was working for Gil Evans. Because I actually played trombone with Howard sitting next to me. That’s what he did. So Howard went in the Gil Evans orchestra. Gil would give him a fairly sophisticated part, but it was a tuba part, based on his writing for tuba and everything. So Howard would take that part and he would expand it. And then Gil heard it. And the next night when Howard came to the book, Gil had re-written the tuba part reflective of what Howard did. And so as Howard evolved the part, Gil evolved his writing for the tuba and realized that the tuba can do so much more. So then he began to write more and more for Howard and then Howard began to expand on that. So if you came in to sub for Howard Johnson in the Gil Evans orchestra — besides having lengthy, not an 8-bar tuba solo, I mean a full expressive tuba solo where you can just express © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-
